column2: A nuclear sub has gone missing. Men are trapped, and time is running out. How can we possibly find them in time?
Watch a search that finds nothing. It has still told you something.
In May of nineteen sixty-eight the United States Navy had to ask that question for real. The U S S Scorpion, a nuclear submarine, was heading home across the Atlantic with ninety-nine men aboard.
She was due at Norfolk, Virginia, on the twenty-seventh, and did not arrive. For nine days the Navy searched the ocean, as if her crew might still be saved.
They could not be. She had gone down five days before she was due, in more than ten thousand feet of water. All ninety-nine men were lost.
At the time, nobody could be sure of that. And even to find the wreck, the Navy faced the first question of any search. Where do you look?
Not everywhere. Take a patch of sea about twelve miles on a side. But the search gear rode a sled, towed just above the sea floor. It saw a strip about two hundred feet wide.
One pass over the whole patch meant thousands of miles of towing. That is several times all the open-sea searching the sled did before the find.
So where would you look first?
The natural answer is, the likeliest place. So you need a map that gives every place its chance.
Start small, with a made-up sea. Four cells, a lost ship, and two stories of what might have happened to it.
In the first story it kept to its route. Then the wreck is most likely in cell A, maybe in B, less likely in C. In the second it strayed, and the wreck could be anywhere.

Now weigh the two stories by how much you believe each one. Say sixty to forty. Then picture a hundred dots, sixty from the first story and forty from the second. Each dot is one place the wreck could be.
The first story puts half of its dots in cell A. The second puts a quarter of its dots there. What is the chance the wreck is in cell A?
Half of sixty is thirty. A quarter of forty is ten. Forty dots in a hundred. Forty percent.
Count every cell that way and you have the map. Forty, thirty, twenty, ten.
The Navy's map was made the same way. A Navy scientist, John Craven, had first tried the idea two years earlier. He was searching for a hydrogen bomb, lost in the sea off Palomares, in Spain.

That bomb was found near where a fisherman watched it fall, but the idea stayed. In July of sixty-eight, Craven and a colleague named Andrews set out nine stories of how the Scorpion might have been lost. They gave each story a weight.
An analyst, Henry Richardson, had a computer play those stories out ten thousand times. Ten thousand dots.
Then he counted the dots in every cell. This is the map they printed.
One cell stands out, with one dot in every eight. They called it E five. Was she there?
Almost. The wreck lay in a neighbouring cell, within two hundred and sixty yards of the edge of E five.
But the map alone did not find her, and the search took five months. To see why, we need a method for using a map like this.
Back to the made-up sea. Forty percent says search cell A first. But a search is not a sure thing.
Cell A is a canyon. A search there sees the wreck only one time in four. In the flat cells, a search sees it two times in three.
So ask a better question. How likely is one search of a cell to find the wreck?
Forty percent, seen one time in four. Thirty percent, seen two times in three. Which cell gives the better chance of a find, A or B?
Cell B. A quarter of forty is ten. Two thirds of thirty is twenty. Twice the chance.
The chance of a find is the chance it is there, times the chance of seeing it. So the best cell to search is not always the likeliest.
So we search cell B. And the search comes back empty.
That is not nothing. Look at the dots. Thirty are in B, and the search would have caught two out of every three. Twenty dots.
If the wreck were at any of those twenty, we would have it. We do not. So they go out.
Eighty dots are left, and the wreck is at one of them. Ten are still in B, because a search can miss.
Ten dots out of eighty. What is the chance it is in cell B now?
One in eight. Twelve and a half percent, down from thirty.
Now look at cell A. Nobody searched it, and nothing in the sea has changed. But forty dots out of eighty is one half. What changed is what we know.
Every cell we did not search grew by a quarter. Forty to fifty. Twenty to twenty-five. Ten to twelve and a half.
That move has a name. Bayes' rule, after Thomas Bayes, an English minister who died in seventeen sixty-one.

As a recipe. Multiply each cell's chance by the chance that the search would come back empty if the wreck were there. One third for cell B, and one for every other cell. Then divide by what is left, eighty, so the map adds up to a hundred again.
Here is the new map. Cell A has half the chance now. But A is the canyon. Where do you search next?
Cell C. In dots, nothing has changed for A or C. A search of A would still catch ten, and a search of C thirteen and a third. Only B has fallen.
Search. Come back empty. Update. Choose again. That loop is the whole method.
Always search where the next search is most likely to find it. Is that really the best you can do?
Yes. Each search of a cell puts out a fixed slice of the first hundred dots. It does not matter what was searched in between. And a cell's slices only shrink.

So the best eight searches are the eight biggest slices, and the rule takes them biggest first. For a wreck that stays put, and searches that are fresh tries of equal effort, no other order is ever ahead.
On the Navy's map the difference is large. Suppose every search sees a wreck in its cell two times in three. One plan has no map, and goes row by row. The other follows the rule.
By the map's own reckoning, twenty searches row by row have less than one chance in a hundred of a find. Twenty by the rule, about one in two. And most of that is the map itself.
Why would a search see a wreck only two times in three? In the Second World War, hunting submarines, Bernard Koopman and his colleagues asked how much of an area a searcher really covers.
With perfect strips, laid side by side, enough track to pass over a cell once would cover all of it.
But if your strips land at random, some overlap and some leave gaps. The same track then covers, on average, sixty-three percent.
Koopman's formula gives that number, and the rest of the curve. A little more track, and you are at two in three. That is one search of a flat cell.
Run that search twice over one cell. The first pass catches six dots of nine. The second is a fresh try, and catches two in three of what is left. How many of the nine are caught?
Eight. One dot in nine is still there, and a third pass leaves one in twenty-seven. Each pass finds less than the one before, and no number of passes makes it certain.
A wreck stays where it is. A person in the water does not. Wind and current carry that person along, and nobody knows either one exactly.
So every dot moves with its own guess at the wind and the current. The map drifts, and it spreads. What does that do to a search?
And a person is hard to see. From a helicopter, the Coast Guard counts on spotting someone in the water only inside a narrow strip. It is a tenth of a mile wide.

Twice the radius is four times the area, so each square mile gets a quarter of the track. In this model, one hour in, a flight would find the person ninety-three times in a hundred. Twelve hours in, the same flight would find that person thirteen times in a hundred. That is why hours matter.

The United States Coast Guard has had software that plans searches this way since nineteen seventy-four. It moves thousands of dots, each a possible drifting person or boat, and updates them by Bayes' rule after every empty search.
In July of twenty thirteen, a lobsterman named John Aldridge fell off his boat at night, about forty miles off Long Island. Nobody saw him go.
The searchers had to guess when he fell, and guessed the evening before. So the first map put its dots almost thirty miles too far north.
The map was wrong because its story was wrong. What could fix it?
Evidence. On deck, his partner found an open hatch, and pumps running. That was work Aldridge usually left until the boat was far offshore. He had fallen hours later.

The Coast Guard ran the map again, and the dots moved south. That afternoon a helicopter flying through those dots spotted him. He was alive, clinging to two lobster buoys, after almost twelve hours in the water.
June, two thousand nine. Air France flight four four seven, from Rio to Paris, went down in the Atlantic. All two hundred and twenty-eight people aboard were killed.
The wreck had to lie inside a circle forty nautical miles in radius. In nearly two years, three underwater searches found nothing.

Then a team of search analysts built a map from three separate stories. They weighted them thirty-five, thirty-five and thirty, the way we weighted two stories. And they updated the map for every empty search.
One search needed a decision. For a month, ships had listened for the beacons on the plane's black boxes, and heard nothing. How much should that silence count?
If the beacons worked, a great deal. If they were broken, not at all. So the analysts drew the map twice, once counting the silence, and once leaving it out.

Both maps put their weight near the centre of the circle. The search resumed there, and found the wreck after about a week. It lay in a high-chance part of the second map, in water the listening ships had already crossed.
The Navy had faced the same question in nineteen sixty-eight. Its map reached the search ship in August, two months into the search. Every pass of the sled since June was then scored against it.
By October, the ship's numbers said one cell had been searched ninety-four percent thoroughly. Of every hundred dots there, ninety-four went out. It was the cell with the wreck in it.
The wreck was there, and the sled had been over that water. What went wrong?
The estimate of how well they were looking. At sea, they believed the sonar could see a strip eight hundred feet wide.
Estimated afterwards against the wreck itself, the sonar that passed her had not seen her at all. The camera and the magnetic detector saw about two hundred feet.
So the better estimate for that cell was sixty-five percent, not ninety-four. And on that estimate, ten more passes with that sonar would have found nothing.
She was found at the end of October. The sled had gone back to where a scrap of metal was photographed that summer, beside the map's top cell.
An empty search only tells you something if it could have found what you were looking for.

Four searches, and where each one ended. Palomares, found near where a fisherman watched it fall. Scorpion, beside the map's top cell. Air France, near the centre both maps pointed to. John Aldridge, inside the dots, once the story was put right.
The strip was believed too wide. The silence might have meant nothing. The story was five hours off. So what does the method ask of you?
The first map does not have to be right. It has to leave room for the truth. You have to judge how well you really looked. And you need a new map when new evidence says a story was wrong.
The ninety-nine men of the Scorpion could not be saved.
The method that searched for them now searches for people who can.
